description: Sabotages for win-time-sys. Run with tools/run-sabotage.ps1; see tools/README-sabotage.md for the format and for why the results are read the way they are.
notCoveredHere: Three defects in the interrupt-time clocks no test can catch. A plain clock reading the precise call is more precise, not wrong: the difference is cost, which WT-1.6's probe measures. A clock reading the other interrupt timeline -- biased for unbiased, or the reverse -- gives identical values on a machine that has never slept, which a CI host need not have done. And QueryUnbiasedInterruptTime's failure, asserted in debug builds, is documented to happen only for a null pointer, which a reference cannot be. Likewise QueryPerformanceCounter's and QueryPerformanceFrequency's, which are documented to always succeed on Windows XP and later. Reading the performance counter's frequency on every call rather than once is not caught either: the frequency is fixed at boot, so it changes what a call costs, never what it answers.

sabotages.name: WT-1.2: points order backwards
sabotages.why: Which of two readings came first is the question most callers ask of a time point.

sabotages.name: WT-1.2: the distance between points has its sign flipped
sabotages.why: Elapsed time would come out negative, and a duration from it would be refused.

sabotages.name: WT-1.2: moving a point forwards does not check the timeline's end
sabotages.why: A point moved past either end would wrap to the other, silently reordering it against every other point.
replace:
let moved = i128::from(self.ticks) + i128::from(ticks.count);
        Some(Self::from_ticks(moved as u64))

sabotages.name: WT-1.2: moving a point backwards moves it forwards
sabotages.why: Subtracting ticks is the opposite of adding them.

sabotages.name: WT-1.2: a backwards distance becomes a duration
sabotages.why: A Duration cannot be negative; converting a backwards distance to its length would hide which way it pointed.

sabotages.name: WT-1.2: a duration drops its fraction of a second
sabotages.why: Interrupt and system time tick every 100 ns; losing the sub-second part loses almost everything a short interval measures.

sabotages.name: WT-1.2: ticks from a duration drop its fraction of a second
sabotages.why: The same loss in the other direction.

sabotages.name: WT-1.2: ticks from a duration too long for them wrap
sabotages.why: A duration that does not fit must be refused, not turned into some other count.

sabotages.name: WT-1.2: negating the most negative distance wraps
sabotages.why: i64::MIN has no opposite; wrapping returns itself, a distance pointing the wrong way.

sabotages.name: WT-1.3: the precise interrupt clock reads the plain one
sabotages.why: A precise clock no finer than the system tick reads the same value across a short interval, which is what a precise clock exists to tell apart. Caught by the test that needs it to advance within a fraction of the finest tick.

sabotages.name: WT-1.3: the precise unbiased clock reads the plain one
sabotages.why: The same, on the unbiased timeline.

sabotages.name: WT-1.3: the plain interrupt clock is frozen
sabotages.why: A reading must be the kernel's, not a constant; caught by the test that needs the plain clock to advance across a tick.

sabotages.name: WT-1.3: interrupt time ticks every microsecond
sabotages.why: Every duration measured on interrupt or system time would be ten times too long.

sabotages.name: WT-1.4: the precise system clock reads the coarse one
sabotages.why: A precise clock no finer than the system tick; caught by the test that needs it to advance within a fraction of the finest tick.

sabotages.name: WT-1.4: the coarse system clock is frozen
sabotages.why: A reading must be the kernel's, not a constant; caught by the test that needs the coarse clock to advance across a tick.

sabotages.name: WT-1.4: a FILETIME's halves are put together the wrong way round
sabotages.why: The count would be meaningless. Caught by the comparison with std's own reading of the same call, and by the test of the halves.

sabotages.name: WT-1.4: a FILETIME's high half is shifted too little
sabotages.why: The high half would overlap the low one; caught by the same two tests.

sabotages.name: WT-1.5: the performance counter's period is twice its frequency
sabotages.why: Every duration measured on the counter would be half its length. Caught by the comparison with the frequency Windows reports and with Instant, which reads the same counter.

sabotages.name: WT-1.5: the performance clock is frozen
sabotages.why: A reading must be the counter's, not a constant.

sabotages.name: CONTROL: the performance count is cast rather than reinterpreted
sabotages.why: The manifest checking itself on code every performance test runs: for a count that is never negative, `as u64` and `cast_unsigned` are the same bits.

sabotages.name: CONTROL: a FILETIME's halves are added rather than or-ed
sabotages.why: The manifest checking itself on code every system-time test runs: the halves cannot overlap, so adding them is or-ing them.

sabotages.name: CONTROL: the plain interrupt clock types its out-parameter
sabotages.why: The manifest checking itself on code every interrupt test runs: the call already makes the out-parameter a u64.

sabotages.name: CONTROL: a backwards distance is tested by its count
sabotages.why: The manifest checking itself: a count below zero is exactly what is_negative tests, so this is an equivalent change on code every duration test runs.
